title: Visit the imprisoned
hookLine: I was in prison and you came to me
tomorrow: why would a man leave a feast to bury a stranger?

lines: TEN EPISODES: DID HE DO IT?
cards: A true-crime podcast can spend ten episodes on one question: did he do it? The comments pick sides by episode two. Now the strange detail in Matthew's Gospel.
The king lists the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and then, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." No charge. No verdict.
Not one word on whether the prisoner was guilty. For a story about the final judgment, that's an odd thing to leave out.

teach.b: The text solves it itself. In that line, the king isn't judging the prisoner. He's judging the visitor.
The question on the table isn't what did he do, but did you come. And the king goes further: I was in prison.
He puts himself inside the cell. The Gospels remember that Jesus was arrested, bound and led away, so the king who says it knows what being held is like.
The letter to the Hebrews says it from the other side: remember prisoners as if you were bound with them. As if you were bound. Not as if you were the jury.
Second Timothy shows what the visit costs. Paul writes from his chains that those in Asia turned away from him.
But one friend, Onesiphorus, came to Rome, searched for him carefully and found him, often refreshed him, and was not ashamed of his chain. Being seen with a prisoner can mark you. He went anyway.
None of this says crimes don't matter; the Catechism keeps a place for justice and punishment. The visit just isn't the courtroom.
The Church names visiting the imprisoned among the corporal works of mercy.

Today it looks like chaplains and volunteers leading prayer behind the walls, pen pals writing to people inside, families making the long drive on visiting day. Not everyone can go in. Anyone can come close.

how: Catholic prison ministries, chaplains and volunteers lead prayer and Bible study inside prisons and jails, and some parishes run letter-writing programs for people in prison.

o: go to people in prison and keep them company
free people who were wrongly locked up
pray only for the guards and the wardens

games.q: inside the puzzle — tap the pairs.
p: I was in prison, and you came to me
as if you were bound with them
the one the king is really judging

s: the king only praises visits to prisoners who were innocent
he never names a charge or a verdict. the question is whether you came.
visiting the imprisoned means pretending crimes don't matter
the Catechism keeps a place for justice. the visit just isn't the courtroom.
the Gospels say Jesus himself was arrested and bound
the king who says I was in prison knows what being held is like.

games.q: a friend's older brother just started a sentence at the county jail. she asks you to help write him a letter, but you've heard what he did. what does the king's line point to?
o: help with the letter; the king asks if you came, not the verdict.
help only after her brother admits to what he did, in writing.
pass; letters like that are for chaplains and close family.
games.why: the king never asks the charge, and Hebrews says to remember prisoners as if bound with them. a letter is one way of coming.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one line you'd want to read if you were inside: no lecture, just company, something like someone thought of you today.
Hold the paper while you sit, and if you pray, you can pray for one person in prison, known or unknown, as if you were there with them.

wordCard.voice: Visit the imprisoned. Come close to someone locked away, in person, by letter or in prayer, without asking for the verdict first.

orig.note: Greek: you came. the king's word for the visit in Matthew 25:36.

carryVoice: Your line: you came to me. The king asked whether you came, not what the prisoner did. See you tomorrow.
